# Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Neonatology > Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn*

[Original Article Link](/library/i40JQT)

---

## Summary

<u>Hemolytic</u> disease of the fetus and <u>newborn</u> (HDFN) is a condition characterized by the destruction of fetal <u>red blood cells</u> (<u>RBC</u>) and subsequent <u>anemia</u>. It is commonly caused by a Rhesus (Rh) or <u>ABO incompatibility</u> between the mother and fetus, although other blood incompatibilities (e.g., Kell <u>blood group incompatibility</u>) and other conditions not caused by red cell <u>alloimmunization</u> (e.g., <u>congenital heart defects</u>) can also cause HDFN. In <u>Rh incompatibility</u>, maternal <u>IgG antibodies</u> form after maternal exposure to fetal <u>Rh-positive</u> blood during <u>birth</u> or <u>potentially sensitizing antepartum events</u>. The initial <u>pregnancy</u> is usually not affected; however, subsequent <u>pregnancies</u> are at risk of fetal <u>hemolysis</u> and, in severe cases, intrauterine <u>hydrops fetalis</u>. <u>ABO incompatibility</u>, on the other hand, may lead to fetal <u>hemolysis</u> in the first <u>pregnancy</u> because of preexisting <u>antibodies</u> in the mother, and it usually has a milder course of disease. <u>Newborns</u> may present with <u>pallor</u>, <u>jaundice</u>, and <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>. Diagnosis of HDFN involves clinical and laboratory assessment for evidence of <u>antibody</u>-mediated <u>hemolysis</u> (e.g., <u>Coombs test</u>). Prenatal imaging may be used to exclude <u>hydrops fetalis</u>. Treatment includes <u>iron</u> supplementation and, in the case of severe <u>jaundice</u>, <u>phototherapy</u>. In rare cases, extremely low <u>hemoglobin</u> (<u>Hb</u>) levels require <u>transfusion</u> of red cell concentrates. Since <u>Rh incompatibility</u> may be fatal, <u>anti-D immunoglobulin</u> (<u>RhIG</u>) is administered to <u>Rh-negative</u> pregnant women. <u>ABO incompatibility</u>, on the other hand, rarely presents with complications and does not require <u>immunoglobulin</u> prophylaxis.

---

## Etiology

* <u>ABO incompatibility</u>: present in ∼ 20% of all <u>pregnancies</u>; however, only 5–10% of <u>newborns</u> from these <u>pregnancies</u> are symptomatic.

* <u>Rh incompatibility</u>: rare following routine <u>anti-D prophylaxis</u>

* <u>Kell blood group system</u> incompatibility: second most common cause of severe HDFN after <u>Rh disease</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u>: maternal exposure to fetal blood during <u>pregnancy</u>  [[1]](/library/VqYGxJ)

* Antenatal procedures (e.g., <u>amniocentesis</u>, <u>cesarean delivery</u>, <u>termination of pregnancy</u>)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>-related complications (e.g., <u>ectopic pregnancy</u>, <u>placental abruption</u>)

* Trauma





References:[[2]](/library/uIapeN)[[3]](/library/qKaChl)

---

## Pathophysiology

### ABO incompatibility [[2]](/library/uIapeN)[[4]](/library/7W145f0)




* Highest risk: mother with <u>blood group</u> O; <u>newborn</u> with <u>blood group</u> A or B

* Maternal <u>antibodies</u> (anti-A and/or anti-B) against nonself <u>antigens</u> of the ABO system are present even if sensitization has not occurred;   , so fetal <u>hemolysis</u> may occur during the first <u>pregnancy</u>.





### Rh incompatibility  [[2]](/library/uIapeN)[[4]](/library/7W145f0)




* <u>Rh-negative</u> mother and <u>Rh-positive</u> fetus ;  [[5]](/library/4nd3tq0)

* Production of maternal <u>IgM antibodies</u> against the Rh <u>antigen</u> ;  occurs after exposure of fetal blood cells to the maternal circulation (fetomaternal hemorrhage) during delivery or an antepartum Rh sensitizing event, e.g.: 

* Threatened or confirmed <u>pregnancy loss</u>

* <u>Termination of pregnancy</u>

* <u>Ectopic pregnancy</u>

* Invasive obstetric procedures

* <u>External cephalic version</u>

* <u>Antepartum hemorrhage</u>

* Abdominal trauma

* Over time, maternal <u>IgM antibodies</u> <u>seroconvert</u> to Rh-<u>IgG</u> (<u>antibodies</u> are able to cross the <u>placenta</u>).

* In a subsequent <u>pregnancy</u> with an <u>Rh-positive</u> fetus: rapid production of maternal <u>IgG</u> <u>anti-D</u> <u>antibodies</u> to fetal <u>RhD antigens</u> → Rh-<u>IgG</u> agglutination of fetal <u>RBCs</u> with <u>hemolytic anemia</u> → risk of HDFN with possible <u>hydrops fetalis</u>

* <u>Rh-incompatibility</u> in combination with <u>ABO incompatibility</u>: reduction of Rh(D)-isoimmunization in <u>Rh-negative</u> mothers





![Rhesus (Rh) incompatibility in pregnancy](media/xwee5fa3kxvikni1grjseknq.jpg)

Rhesus (Rh) incompatibility in pregnancy




### <u>Kell blood group system</u> incompatibility [[6]](/library/Gm1BSh0)[[7]](/library/Em18hh0)




* The <u>Kell blood group system</u> includes K (K1), k (K2), Kp<sup>a</sup>, Kp<sup>b</sup>, Js<sup>a</sup>, and Js<sup>b</sup><u>antigens</u> (for more information, see “<u>Kell antigen system</u>”), which can trigger substantial <u>immune responses</u>.

* Responsible for up to 10% of severe cases of HDFN [[8]](/library/Fm1ghh0)

* Maternal exposure to Kell <u>antigen</u> in previous <u>pregnancy</u> through the <u>placenta</u> or through <u>blood transfusions</u> → sensitization and production of maternal <u>anti-Kell antibodies</u> → <u>antibodies</u> enter circulation of Kell-positive fetus through <u>placenta</u> → destruction of fetal <u>RBC</u> precursors and mature <u>RBCs</u> → ↓ production of <u>RBCs</u> and ↑ <u>hemolysis</u> → severe fetal <u>anemia</u>

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Nonimmune hydrops fetalis [[9]](/library/qjXCYy)




* Definition: a subgroup of <u>hemolytic</u> diseases of the fetus and <u>newborn</u> not caused by red cell <u>alloimmunization</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Incidence</u>: ∼ 1 in 4,000 <u>pregnancies</u>

* Accounts for over 90% of all <u>hydrops fetalis</u> cases

* Etiology

* <u>Congenital heart defects</u> and <u>arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Chromosomal aberrations</u> (e.g., <u>Turner syndrome</u>, <u>Down syndrome</u>, <u>trisomy 18</u>)

* Severe fetal <u>anemia</u> (e.g., <u>thalassemia</u>, <u>twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome</u>, <u>fetomaternal hemorrhage</u>)

* <u>Congenital TORCH infections</u> (especially <u>parvovirus B19</u> infection)

* Pathophysiology: severe fetal <u>anemia</u> → <u>hypoxia</u> →;  ↓ hepatic and <u>renal blood flow</u>  → activation of <u>RAAS</u> → ↑ central venous pressure and ↓ lymphatic flow → fetal <u>edema</u> [[10]](/library/FScgYX0)

---

## Clinical features

### Prenatal



* <u>Hydrops fetalis</u> (expected in cases of <u>Rh incompatibility</u> and in <u>nonimmune hydrops fetalis</u>)




### Postnatal




* Neonatal <u>anemia</u>

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* <u>Neonatal jaundice</u>

* Usually present at <u>birth</u> or manifests within the first 24 hours of life

* In <u>Rh incompatibility</u>, <u>unconjugated bilirubin</u> levels may be dangerously high, causing <u>kernicterus</u>.

* <u>Hypoxia</u>

* <u>Prematurity</u>

* Scattered <u>petechiae</u> (rare but associated with poor prognosis) [[11]](/library/IjXYby)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>ABO incompatibility</u> usually has a significantly milder course of disease than <u>Rh incompatibility</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Anemia</u> may conceal <u>cyanosis</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

The diagnosis of HDFN requires <u>evidence of hemolysis</u> in the presence of fetomaternal blood incompatibility.




### Prenatal diagnosis



* Imaging

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: to determine <u>hydrops fetalis</u> 

* Fetal pleural or <u>pericardial effusions</u>

* Fetal <u>ascites</u>

* Fetal subcutaneous or nuchal <u>edema</u>

* <u>Placental</u> <u>edema</u>

* Doppler <u>sonography</u> of fetal <u>blood vessels</u>: Increased flow rate indicates fetal <u>anemia</u>.




![Hydrops fetalis](media/oxnaqeeooc0160k1zw5dytcz.jpg)

Hydrops fetalis




### Postnatal diagnosis



* If the <u>newborn</u> has signs of <u>hemolysis</u>, conduct a <u>Coombs test</u> (either direct or indirect).

* <u>Rh incompatibility</u>: positive

* <u>ABO incompatibility</u>: weak positive or negative

---

## Differential diagnoses

### ABO vs. Rh incompatibility




|  | <u>ABO incompatibility</u> | <u>Rh incompatibility</u> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Incidence</u> | <br>* Common<br><br> | <br>* Rare<br><br> |
| Disease during the first <u>pregnancy</u> | <br>* Common<br><br> | <br>* Rare<br><br> |
| Clinical symptoms | <br>* Generally normal to mild; may be asymptomatic<br><br> | <br>* Mild to severe<br><br> |
| <u>Coombs test</u> (direct or indirect) | <br>* Weak positive or negative<br><br> | <br>* Positive<br><br> |
| <u>Spherocytosis</u> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Rare<br><br> |





### Differential diagnoses of <u>petechiae</u> in <u>newborns</u>




#### Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia




* Description: a rare condition in <u>newborns</u> characterized by maternal-fetal <u>platelet</u> incompatibility resulting in fetal <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: the leading cause of severe <u>thrombocytopenia</u> in the <u>newborn</u>

* Pathophysiology: formation of maternal <u>antibodies</u> against fetal <u>platelets</u> (most commonly targeting <u>platelet</u> <u>antigen</u> 1a) → maternal <u>IgG</u> cross the <u>placenta</u> and result in the destruction of fetal <u>platelets</u> → fetal and neonatal <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* Clinical features

* Mild: asymptomatic <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* Moderate: petechia and/or <u>ecchymoses</u> within a few hours after <u>birth</u>

* Severe: spontaneous <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>





#### Other




* <u>Immune thrombocytopenic purpura</u>

* <u>Kasabach-Meritt syndrome</u>

* <u>Perinatal</u> infections

* For an overview of <u>thrombocytopenias</u> and disorders of <u>platelet</u> function, see “<u>Differential diagnosis of platelet disorders</u>.”





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

* All patients

* Refer to specialists, e.g., <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u>, for management.

* Consider repeat <u>titers</u> in patients with a positive RhD screen, as prior <u>RhIG</u> administration can lead to <u>false positives</u>.  [[13]](/library/GOdBFJ0)

* Prenatal

* Intrauterine <u>blood transfusion</u> via the <u>umbilical vein</u>, <u>umbilical artery</u>, <u>peritoneal cavity</u>, or <u>heart</u> (should only be performed in centers with experience in fetal <u>transfusions</u>.)

* Possible <u>IV immunoglobulin</u> (IVIG) in severe cases

* Early delivery in severely affected <u>pregnancies</u>

* Postnatal

* <u>Anemia</u>: <u>iron</u> supplementation and, if necessary, <u>RBC</u> <u>transfusion</u>.  [[14]](/library/wIahUN)

* <u>Hyperbilirubinemia</u>: <u>phototherapy</u>; if necessary, <u>exchange transfusion</u> with <u>red blood cells</u>

* See “Treatment” in <u>neonatal jaundice</u>.

* In severe cases, <u>IV immunoglobulin</u> (IVIG) may be administered.





> [!TIP]
> Previous administration of <u>RhIG</u> may cause <u>false-positive</u> <u>anti-D</u> <u>antibodies</u>. [[13]](/library/GOdBFJ0)

---

## Prevention

Of the <u>causes of HDFN</u>, only RhD incompatibility has a proven prophylactic treatment (i.e., <u>RhIG</u>). [[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)




### Screening for RhD alloimmunization in pregnancy [[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)[[16]](/library/9ndNvq0)




* All <u>pregnancies</u>: Perform routine maternal <u>ABO typing</u> and <u>Rh typing</u> at the <u>initial prenatal visit</u>.

* <u>RhD-positive</u> pregnant individuals: Further screening is not indicated; provide <u>routine prenatal care</u>.

* <u>RhD-negative</u> pregnant individuals: Screen for <u>anti-D</u> <u>antibodies</u> with an <u>indirect antiglobulin test</u>. ;  [[12]](/library/nfW75k0)

* <u>Anti-D</u> <u>titers</u> positive (sensitized): Refer to <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u> for <u>treatment of alloimmunization in pregnancy</u>.  [[12]](/library/nfW75k0)[[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)

* <u>Anti-D</u> negative (not sensitized): See “<u>Management of unsensitized RhD-negative individuals during pregnancy</u>.” [[17]](/library/LldwxJ0)





> [!TIP]
> Discuss patients with RhD variants (partial D and weak D) with a specialist; treatment with <u>anti-D immunoglobulin</u> may be required. [[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)




> [!TIP]
> If paternity is certain (e.g., <u>IVF</u>) and paternal <u>Rh type</u> is negative, pregnant <u>RhD-negative</u> individuals do not require additional screening, testing, or <u>RhIG</u>. Paternal <u>Rh typing</u> is not routine; the cost is similar to <u>RhIG</u>, and there is a potential for discrepancy between the reported father and biological father. [[12]](/library/nfW75k0)[[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)




### Management of unsensitized RhD-negative individuals during pregnancy [[12]](/library/nfW75k0)[[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)




* Educate patients to seek care immediately after <u>potentially Rh-sensitizing events</u>.

* Give <u>RhIG</u> as indicated.

* Routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Within 72 hours of <u>Rh-sensitizing events</u> (including <u>invasive prenatal diagnostic testing</u>)

* At delivery if <u>newborn</u> blood tests show the <u>infant</u> is <u>RhD-positive</u>

* Reassess for sensitization at 24–28 weeks' <u>gestation</u> and before each dose of <u>RhIG</u> (if feasible).  [[12]](/library/nfW75k0)[[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)





> [!WARNING]
> If repeat screening shows the patient is now sensitized, do not give <u>RhIG</u>; start <u>treatment of alloimmunization in pregnancy</u>. [[12]](/library/nfW75k0)




> [!TIP]
> If fetal noninvasive cell-free <u>DNA</u> testing shows the fetus is <u>RhD-negative</u>, <u>RhIG</u> is not required; however, the test is not routinely performed because of cost and the high rate of inconclusive results. [[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)




#### Anti-D immunoglobulin (<u>RhIG</u>)




* Given to unsensitized <u>RhD-negative</u> pregnant individuals to prevent <u>Rh-sensitization</u>

* Rapidly clears <u>Rh-positive</u> <u>erythrocytes</u>, preventing the development of <u>anti-D</u> <u>antibodies</u> [[18]](/library/lLdvBq0)

* <u>Dosages of RhIG</u> are usually fixed, but <u>fetomaternal hemorrhage tests</u> may be needed to determine if larger doses are required.





> [!TIP]
> <u>RhIG</u> protects fetuses in subsequent <u>pregnancies</u>. [[15]](/library/eqYxxJ)




##### Fetomaternal hemorrhage tests




* Indications

* <u>Rh-sensitizing events</u> > 20 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* After delivery of a <u>RhD-positive</u> fetus

* Initial testing: rosette test to qualitatively detect <u>fetal-maternal hemorrhage</u>

* Subsequent testing (if positive <u>rosette test</u>): Kleihauer-Betke test ;  (most common) or <u>flow cytometry</u>

* Quantitative tests that calculate fetal blood in the maternal circulation

* Used to determine <u>RhIG</u> dosing
